claims.text: W, Ta, and Mo are high-activation refractory elements, whereas V, Cr, Ti, and Zr are lower-activation alternatives.
Replacing or minimizing W, Ta, and Mo with V, Cr, Ti, or Zr in a refractory HEA will reduce its long-term radioactivity.
The modified low-activation refractory HEA will retain the high-temperature mechanical strength needed for fusion plasma-facing components.
The modified low-activation refractory HEA will retain the irradiation resistance needed for fusion plasma-facing components.
A conventional W-Ta-Cr-V-based refractory HEA can have a nanocrystalline, multiphase initial state.
The W-Ta-Cr-V HEA has high mechanical strength.
The W-Ta-Cr-V HEA resists irradiation-induced loop and helium-bubble formation under ion irradiation.
Fusion plasma-facing components must operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K under large heat loads and exposure to plasma species and neutrons.
The modified alloy can preserve a single-phase or stable multiphase BCC structure and nanocrystalline morphology under irradiation.
A nanocrystalline refractory HEA can exhibit low defect generation and evolution, irradiation-induced grain refinement, and no detectable grain growth.
Substituting lower-activation elements for higher-activation elements causes fewer long-lived radioisotopes to form during neutron irradiation.
A nanostructured grain matrix inhibits irradiation-defect coarsening.
Inhibiting irradiation-defect coarsening maintains mechanical integrity.
Nanocrystalline refractory HEAs can maintain radiation tolerance under heavy-ion, dual-beam, and helium-implantation conditions.
The modified alloy will have significantly lower residual radioactivity after prolonged neutron exposure than conventional W-containing alloys.
The modified alloy will achieve acceptable high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
Tungsten is a leading plasma-facing material because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rate, and low tritium retention.
Conventional W-based alloys and refractory HEAs containing high-activation elements suffer from long-term radioactive activation under fusion conditions.
Composition must be balanced so that reducing activation does not compromise melting temperature, phase stability, or mechanical properties.
